bib.title: Python for Data Analysis, 2nd ed., Chapter 1: Preliminaries

question: What is the book about, why use Python for data analysis, and which libraries and setup does it assume?
contributions: Scope: structured data (tabular, arrays, keyed tables, time series)
Overview of NumPy, pandas, matplotlib, IPython/Jupyter, SciPy, scikit-learn, statsmodels
Install and setup with Anaconda, Python 3.6

results.claim: pandas has two primary objects: DataFrame (tabular, column-oriented, row and column labels) and Series (one-dimensional labeled array).
results.quote: The primary objects in pandas that will be used in this book are the DataFrame,
results.note: Sentence continues on next lines: a tabular, column-oriented data structure with both row and column labels, and the Series, a one-dimensional labeled array object.

results.claim: pandas was motivated by labeled axes with automatic or explicit data alignment, which prevents errors from misaligned, differently indexed data.
results.setup: McKinney's list of requirements when he started building pandas at AQR Capital Management in early 2008
results.quote: Data structures with labeled axes supporting automatic or explicit data alignment

results.claim: Other listed pandas design requirements: integrated time series, same structures for time series and non-time series, metadata-preserving arithmetic and reductions, flexible missing-data handling, SQL-style merge/relational operations.
results.quote: Arithmetic operations and reductions that preserve metadata

limits: Orientation chapter with no data, benchmarks or experiments; claims are the author's opinion.
Dated 2017: Python 3.6, Anaconda 4.1, Python 2 EOL 2020, IPython/Jupyter history stops at 2017, library counts as of 2017.
practices: Use the Anaconda distribution and Python 3.6 or higher (1.4).
Install with conda first, then pip; do not update conda packages with pip (1.4).
Do not use from numpy import *; use the np/pd/plt import conventions (1.6).
Work in IPython or Jupyter for execute-explore iteration plus a text editor (1.4).
Treat matplotlib as the default visualization tool (1.3).
Optimize only computational bottlenecks; glue code is rarely worth it (1.2).
